newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia under pressure to maintain media diversity.
newsitem.headline: Australia under pressure to maintain media diversity.

text.p: The Australian government faced mounting pressure on Monday to maintain media ownership limits, with a public appeal to the prime minister from leading Australians and the threat of a parliamentary media inquiry.
About 80 prominent Australians, including politicians, artists, clergy and community leaders, published an open letter to Prime Minister John Howard to protect media diversity.
Howard has signalled his government could ease cross-media ownership limits, possibly announcing the changes this week.
"We urge you not to allow media ownership to fall into fewer hands," said the open letter published in The Australian national newspaper on Monday.

"The ownership of Australia's newspapers, television and radio stations is already among the most concentrated in the world," said the group, which includes former Liberal prime minister Malcolm Fraser, Aboriginal singer Christine Anu and scriptwriter of Academy award winning move Shine, Jan Sardi.
Australia's major newspapers are owned by just two companies -- John Fairfax Holdings Ltd and Rupert Murdoch's News Corp Ltd.
Howard has indicated a review of ownership rules, due to be considered by cabinet this week, may lead to an easing of limits on cross-media holdings in newspapers and the electronic media.
Existing rules set up by the former Labor government prevent a television station holding more than 15 percent of a major newspaper in the same market and vice versa.

The restrictions prevent Australia's richest man Kerry Packer, who owns the television and magazine Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd, from increasing his 12 percent Fairfax stake and taking over the company.
Media and share market speculation is that Packer will make a move on Fairfax if the cross-media rules are relaxed.
Seven television boss Kerry Stokes has accused Howard of striking a unspecified deal with Packer. Howard denies any deal.

The Fairfax-owned Australian Financial Review has reported that Howard had tried to broker an arrangement whereby News Corp could raise its Seven stake if it backed an easing of ownership limits to allow Packer to take over Fairfax. Howard has also denied that charge.
Cheryl Kernot, the leader of the small but influential Australian Democrats Party, said on Monday she supported a parliamentary inquiry into the allegations.
Kernot, a signatory of the open letter, said the government must publicly explain any change to the laws and clear the air over the allegations of deal-making.
"Media ownership is not the gift of prime ministers, or shouldn't be the gift of prime ministers to bestow as favours in return for favourable publicity," Kernot said.
Howard does not have a majority in parliament's upper house, the Senate, and the Democrats could force an inquiry with the backing of the Labor opposition, minor parties and independents.
